# «ОН ЕЩЁ НЕ УШЁЛ» — production bible

60-second vertical short film. Instagram Reels / YouTube Shorts.
Built to run through `scripts/factory.py` on fal.ai.

---

## 0. Director's decisions before a single frame is generated

Five calls that shape everything below. Each one exists because of something
this pipeline has already been burned by.

### 0.1 No text is ever generated by the model

The script needs Russian on-screen text. Video models render text badly and
Cyrillic worse — you get plausible-looking gibberish, and it is the single
fastest way to make a film read as AI-made.

**Every generation prompt below carries `no text, no captions, no signage,
no logos, no watermark`.** All titles, slide headings, phone screens and the
closing cards are burned in afterwards with ffmpeg. Clean plates in, typography
on top. This also means text can be rewritten without paying to regenerate.

The one exception is the laptop/projector screens, which are described as
*abstract charts and coloured blocks, no readable text* — legible-looking
shapes without letterforms.

### 0.2 The flashbacks do NOT de-age him

The script asks for "a younger version of himself". Do not attempt this.
De-aging is the most reliable way to break a likeness, and this film depends on
the audience believing it is the same man in every frame — that is the whole
emotional mechanism.

**Instead the past is signalled by grade and wardrobe, not by face:**

| Signal | Present | Past |
|---|---|---|
| Grade | neutral → cold | warm, lifted blacks, heavier grain |
| Wardrobe | charcoal suit, ID badge | light blue shirt, sleeves rolled, **no jacket, no badge** |
| Aspect | full frame | slight vignette, softer lens |

Same face, same age, different decade. The audience reads it instantly and the
likeness never has to survive a transformation.

### 0.3 Shoot 9:16 natively — never crop from 16:9

Reels and Shorts are vertical. Cropping a 16:9 generation to 9:16 throws away
the composition you paid for and pushes the subject off-centre. Every prompt is
written for a vertical frame: subject placed in the upper-middle third, negative
space below for burned-in text.

### 0.4 Generate 4 seconds, use 1–3

Most shots in this film are cuts of 1.5–3 seconds. The models' minimum is 4s.
Generate 4s and cut in post — the extra footage gives you a choice of frames
and costs nothing extra. Only the three held shots (S01, S23, S29) use their
full length.

### 0.5 Model routing per shot, not one model for the film

Using the routing table in `fal-master-prompt.md` §5:

- **Veo 3.1** ($0.15/s) — the 6 shots where a micro-expression carries the
  scene. Strongest face fidelity, and the whole film dies if his face drifts.
- **Kling 3.0** ($0.126/s) — everything else: environment, inserts, hands,
  wide shots. Cheapest, and face fidelity matters less when he is small in frame
  or absent.
- **Seedance** — not used. Nothing here needs physics simulation, and it costs
  2.4× Kling. Spending it on a film with no explosions would be waste.

## 1. The protagonist

### 1.1 Which face

**Option A (recommended): use the canonical reference already in the project.**
`identity.canonical_face_ref` in `scripts/config.json` points at an approved
still of a Central Asian man in roughly the right age bracket, already proven to
hold across generations. It is paid for, tested, and removes the hardest problem
in the film on day one. If this is your own face and the film is going out under
your name, it also makes the story land harder.

**Option B: a fictional protagonist.** Generate one canonical portrait first
(3 variants, $0.45), approve it, point `canonical_face_ref` at it, and treat it
as the single source of truth for all 29 shots. Do not skip this step and
generate each shot from the text description alone — that is how you end up with
29 different men.

### 1.2 CHARACTER_LOCK — paste verbatim, never paraphrase

```
A Central Asian man of exactly 40 years, short black hair combed back
with faint grey at the temples, thick dark eyebrows, brown eyes with fine
lines at the outer corners, straight nose, defined but soft jawline,
clean-shaven with a faint shadow, light olive skin with natural visible
pores and real skin texture, medium athletic build
```

### 1.3 WARDROBE — two states only

```
PRESENT:  a charcoal-grey wool two-piece suit over a white shirt with the
          collar open and no tie, a plain steel watch on a dark brown
          leather strap on his left wrist, a company ID badge on a navy
          lanyard, carrying a slim dark-grey laptop

PAST:     a light blue shirt with the sleeves rolled to the forearm, no
          jacket, no tie, no ID badge, the same steel watch on a dark
          brown leather strap
```

The watch is the continuity anchor across both states. It is the one object
present in the first shot and the last.

### 1.4 NEGATIVES — appended to every prompt

```
no text, no captions, no subtitles, no signage, no readable letters, no
logos, no watermark, do not alter the face, no change to facial structure,
no beautification, no age change, no de-aging, no extra fingers, no warped
hands, no duplicate people, no twins, no plastic skin, no exaggerated
expression, no crying, no melodrama, no cartoon look, no floating objects
```

### 1.5 IDENTITY_LOCK — the sentence that goes inside every motion prompt

```
His face stays identical to the first frame throughout — same features,
same proportions, no morphing, no re-lighting of facial structure.
```

Not only in the character block. Inside the motion description too. This exact
phrasing recurs in every reference clip that held its likeness.

---

## 2. Visual grammar

| Act | Seconds | Grade | Camera |
|---|---|---|---|
| I — Belonging | 0–5 | warm, balanced, gentle contrast | slow push to face |
| II — Who he was | 5–13 | warm, lifted blacks, visible grain | handheld weight, shallow |
| III — The change | 13–22 | cooling, desaturating | static, wide, observational |
| IV — Invisible | 22–35 | cold, low saturation, grey-blue | locked off; he is small in frame |
| V — Decision | 35–43 | coldest point of the film | slow push to hands, then face |
| VI — Leaving | 43–50 | cold but softening, practical lamps | static; camera does not follow him |
| VII — Freedom | 50–55 | warm natural daylight returns | camera follows him for the first time |
| VIII — Consequence | 55–60 | neutral, fluorescent, flat | one slow push to the empty chair |

**The camera is an observer, not a participant.** One move per shot, never two.
It follows him only once — in Act VII, after he leaves. That is the visual
payoff: the film starts watching him only when the company stops.

## 3. Shot list

29 shots, 29 final videos — sharing a still does not reduce that count, it only
means two shots animate from one already-paid, already-approved image instead of
generating a second one. `K` = Kling 3.0, `V` = Veo 3.1. `s` = generated seconds
(cut in post). **Still** names which image-generation setup each shot's start
frame comes from — this is the column that controls cost, and it is generated
**once per name, not once per row.**

| # | Time | Shot | Model | s | Still | Variants |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S01 | 0–5 | Elevator opens, he steps out, pauses, small controlled smile | **V** | 6 | `A` solo | 3 |
| S02 | 5–7 | PAST: teaching a younger colleague at a monitor | K | 4 | `B` shared | 3 |
| S03 | 7–8.5 | PAST: he solves it, colleagues exhale with relief | K | 4 | `B` *(reuses S02's image)* | — |
| S04 | 8.5–10 | PAST: presenting to an attentive conference room | K | 4 | `C` solo | 3 |
| S05 | 10–11.5 | PAST: launch event, he stands beside the screen | K | 4 | `D` solo | 3 |
| S06 | 11.5–12.5 | INSERT: his hands on old printed product specs | K | 4 | `E` insert, no face | 1 |
| S07 | 12.5–13 | INSERT: old team photographs spread on a desk | K | 4 | `F` insert, no face | 1 |
| S08 | 13–16 | PRESENT: exec meeting wide, expat presenting, he at the table edge | K | 4 | `G` shared | 3 |
| S09 | 16–19 | He raises his hand slightly; leader gives a small "later" gesture | K | 4 | `G` *(reuses S08's image)* | — |
| S10 | 19–22 | His hand lowers; expression barely changes | **V** | 4 | `H` solo | 3 |
| S11 | 22–24 | He speaks. The room stays silent | K | 4 | `I` shared | 3 |
| S12 | 24–26.5 | Another exec repeats it. Everyone engages | K | 4 | `I` *(reuses S11's image)* | — |
| S13 | 26.5–28 | INSERT: strategy slide, his name absent | K | 4 | `J` insert, no face | 1 |
| S14 | 28–30 | Expat congratulated; he is background, out of focus | K | 4 | `K2` solo, low risk | 1 |
| S15 | 30–31.5 | INSERT: the new corner office, door open | K | 4 | `L` insert, no face | 1 |
| S16 | 31.5–33 | He works alone at his desk, small in a wide frame | K | 4 | `M` solo | 3 |
| S17 | 33–35 | Celebration. He watches from the audience. Push to face | **V** | 6 | `N` solo | 3 |
| S18 | 35–39 | Meeting. Screen behind. He looks around; nobody looks back | K | 6 | `O` solo | 3 |
| S19 | 39–43 | He closes his notebook slowly. Hands, then face | **V** | 6 | `P` solo | 3 |
| S20 | 43–45 | Evening. Almost-empty office. He packs | K | 4 | `Q` shared | 3 |
| S21 | 45–47 | Drawer opens: old ID badge and a photograph | K | 4 | `R` insert, no face | 1 |
| S22 | 47–49 | He looks at the photo. Faint smile. Sets it down | **V** | 4 | `S` solo | 3 |
| S23 | 49–50 | He walks out of frame. Camera holds on the empty desk | K | 6 | `Q` *(reuses S20's image)* | — |
| S24 | 50–52 | Morning. He exits the building, stops, looks back | K | 4 | `T` shared | 3 |
| S25 | 52–54 | Phone vibrates. He reads. He smiles | **V** | 4 | `U` solo | 3 |
| S26 | 54–55 | He pockets the phone and walks. Camera follows | K | 4 | `T` *(reuses S24's image)* | — |
| S27 | 55–57 | Inside: the product is failing. The new exec is lost | K | 4 | `V2` shared, no protagonist | 3 |
| S28 | 57–58 | A senior manager looks around the room. Silence | K | 4 | `V2` *(reuses S27's image)* | — |
| S29 | 58–60 | Slow push to the empty chair. The ID badge is still there. HOLD | K | 6 | `W` insert, no face | 1 |

**23 still-generation setups cover all 29 shots.** Six pairs (`B`, `G`, `I`, `Q`,
`T`, `V2`) share an image across two shots — legitimate because both shots in
each pair are the same location, the same moment, continuing straight into each
other (e.g. S20 packing → S23 the same desk after he's walked out of it). Six
inserts (`E F J L R W`) have no face in frame at all — the identity-lock check
that justifies generating 3 variants doesn't apply to a hand, a slide, or an
empty chair, so those generate once. `S14` is marked low-risk (out of focus,
background) and also generates once rather than three.

**Do not generate any of these twice.** One `still` call per named setup,
approve it, then reuse its URL as the `--start-frame` for every shot that lists
that letter.

## 4. Generation prompts

Every prompt is assembled as:

```
{CHARACTER_LOCK}, {WARDROBE}, in {LOCATION}, {FRAMING}, {ANGLE},
{LIGHT}, {LENS}, {MOOD}, {NEGATIVES}
```

and every **motion** prompt ends with `{IDENTITY_LOCK}`.

Below, `[CL]` = CHARACTER_LOCK, `[W-NOW]` / `[W-PAST]` = wardrobe, `[NEG]` =
negatives, `[IL]` = identity lock. Substitute them literally.

---

### S01 — The arrival *(Veo, 6s)*

**Still:**
> `[CL]`, `[W-NOW]`, standing just outside a stainless-steel elevator in a
> modern corporate headquarters lobby, vertical 9:16 composition with him in the
> upper-middle third and empty polished floor below, medium shot, frontal with a
> slight 10-degree off-axis turn, warm early-morning daylight from tall windows
> camera-left with soft falloff, 50mm lens, shallow depth of field, blurred
> colleagues crossing behind him, quiet and composed with a trace of sadness in
> the eyes, photorealistic cinematic film still, `[NEG]`

**Motion:**
> The elevator doors finish opening behind him and he steps forward one pace,
> then stops. His eyes move slowly across the office. A very small, controlled
> smile forms and fades. Colleagues walk past him in the blurred background
> without looking at him. Camera pushes in slowly and steadily toward his face
> over the full duration, ending on a medium close-up. No other movement.
> Soft office ambience. `[IL]`

## 5. Post-production

### 5.1 Russian on-screen text — burned in, never generated

| Cue | In | Out | Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | 3.0s | 5.0s | `25 лет в компании.` |
| T2 | 11.5s | 13.0s | `Он помогал строить то, чем стала компания.` |
| T3 | 27.0s | 28.0s | `НОВАЯ ПРОДУКТОВАЯ СТРАТЕГИЯ` *(on the S13 slide)* |
| T4 | 36.5s | 38.5s | `«Нам нужны свежие силы.»` |
| T5 | 52.5s | 54.0s | `Мы рады предложить вам должность руководителя…` |
| T6 | 60.0s | 62.0s | `Некоторые преданные сотрудники уходят не по своей воле.` |
| T7 | 62.0s | 64.0s | `Их теряют из-за неверных решений.` |
| T8 | 64.0s | 67.0s | `Талант — не всегда новый.` `Иногда это тот, кого перестали замечать.` |

T6–T8 sit on a black card after the picture cuts. **T8 must hold at least 3
seconds** — it is the line the film is for, and the one people screenshot.

Burn-in with ffmpeg (`drawtext`), using a font that actually has Cyrillic
glyphs — otherwise every letter renders as an empty box.

**Verified in this container:** `/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf`
renders Cyrillic correctly (tested — «25 лет в компании.» came out clean). Check
on any other machine with `fc-list :lang=ru family | head` before rendering.

```bash
FONT=/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf

ffmpeg -i cut.mp4 -vf "drawtext=fontfile=$FONT:\
text='25 лет в компании.':fontcolor=white:fontsize=54:\
x=(w-text_w)/2:y=h*0.78:alpha='if(lt(t,3),0,if(lt(t,3.3),(t-3)/0.3,\
if(lt(t,4.7),1,if(lt(t,5),(5-t)/0.3,0))))'" -c:a copy out.mp4
```

The `alpha` expression fades in over 0.3s, holds, fades out over 0.3s — text
that hard-cuts on and off reads as cheap.

Two gotchas, both hit while testing this:
- Grabbing a **single frame** to check the result needs `-update 1`, or ffmpeg
  refuses and asks for a `%03d` filename pattern.
- Pull that check frame from **inside the hold window**, not `t=0` — at t=0 the
  fade-in puts alpha at zero and you get a blank frame and think it broke.

### 5.2 Grade

`factory.py polish` already carries a filmic grade. Per-act variation is a
per-clip `eq` adjustment before assembly:

```bash
# Act II (past)  — warm, lifted, grainy
--grade-extra "eq=saturation=1.20:gamma_r=1.06:gamma_b=0.95,noise=alls=9:allf=t"
# Acts IV–VI     — cold, drained
--grade-extra "eq=saturation=0.72:gamma_b=1.07:contrast=1.10"
# Act VII        — warm daylight returns
--grade-extra "eq=saturation=1.15:gamma_r=1.05"
```

### 5.3 Assembly

```bash
python3 scripts/factory.py assemble --clips work/film/clips --out work/film/cut.mp4
```

`assemble` now normalises audio across clips — a clip without an audio track no
longer silently strips audio from every other clip. Name clips `01.mp4`,
`02.mp4`, … in cut order.

### 5.4 QC before delivery

```bash
python3 scripts/factory.py frames --file work/film/cut.mp4 --count 12 --out work/film/qc
```

Check all twelve against the canonical reference: face shape, nose, jaw,
eyebrows. **Any shot where he reads as a different man is a failed shot** — it
breaks the one thing the film depends on. Re-run it rather than shipping it.

---

## 6. Budget

The plan below generates **every shot exactly once.** Nothing here is doubled
on purpose — the numbers already assume a clean run, and the only thing that
adds a second generation is a shot that genuinely fails review (§6.1).

| Item | Detail | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Stills | 23 setups (not 29) — 6 shared pairs + 6 no-face inserts generate once, §3 | $8.25 |
| Motion tests | 6 shots with real subtle-acting risk: S09, S10, S17, S19, S22, S25 | $0.72 |
| Finals | All 29 shots, one generation each — 6 Veo (30s total) + 23 Kling (98s total) | $16.85 |
| **Plan total, one pass** | | **$25.82** |

This is not the number quoted the first time this document was written
($26.56) despite covering strictly less redundant work — that number was
**wrong**, not conservative: it counted 26 final videos when the shot list
actually has 29. This version prices what is actually being generated.

### 6.1 What actually costs extra — and what doesn't

Sharing stills and skipping variants on faceless inserts removes real waste.
It does **not** remove the one thing that legitimately costs more than plan: a
shot where the delivered take doesn't hold up on review (`factory.py frames`
against the canonical reference, per §5.4) and has to be run again. That is not
double-generating by habit — it's the one case where a second generation buys
something the first one didn't.

If **every** face-critical shot needed one reshoot (worst realistic case, not
the expected one): +6 finals ≈ +$3.20, landing near **$29**. That is the outer
bound, not the plan.

**Fund $30.** That is the real plan cost plus room for the reshoots that
sometimes turn out to be necessary — not a buffer for regenerating things that
already worked.

---

## 7. Risks, stated plainly

1. **29 shots of face consistency is the hardest thing this pipeline has
   attempted.** The previous film was 3 shots and needed several attempts. Expect
   to reshoot several, and QC every one against the canonical reference.
2. **Two people in frame doubles the failure rate.** S02, S09, S12, S14, S27
   involve a second person; models drift faces and occasionally duplicate people.
   Keep the second person turned away, out of focus, or partially framed.
3. **The "later" gesture in S09 is subtle enough that models may over-play it**
   into something rude. That would break the film's thesis — the antagonist is
   blindness, not cruelty. Motion-test this shot specifically and reject any take
   where the leader looks dismissive rather than distracted.
4. **A 60s film cut from 4s generations means ~26 cuts.** Pace and rhythm are
   decided in the edit, not in generation. Budget real editing time.
5. **FLUX 3** would allow 20s continuous takes and would suit the held shots
   (S23, S29) well — but its fal schema is not yet verified and it costs
   $0.17–0.29/s. Not used here. Worth one test call once there is balance.

---

## 8. What this film must not become

The script is explicit and it is right: **the expatriates are not villains.**
Every prompt above describes them as professional, competent and warm. If a take
makes them smug or cold, it is a failed take — not because it is unkind, but
because it collapses the film into a grievance and destroys the actual thesis:

> The problem is not where talent comes from.
> The problem is when an organisation stops seeing the talent it already has.

The final image carries the whole argument, and it contains no people at all.
An empty chair and a badge nobody picked up.
